linked_lists.notes: Node and LinkedList classes are used before B11 teaches classes: entry topics carry pending concept:classes and present the class lines as a copied template. Making the list iterable with __iter__/yield and __repr__ (Boot.dev) was left to B11 dunder_methods. Step-count comparisons carry pending concept:complexity_big_o (B14). Doubly linked lists were not given a topic. Reconciliation: Node/LinkedList are now taught classes (pending concept:classes resolved to constructors.init_sets_attributes); long examples trimmed to the changed lines. reverse_in_place kept: a distinct, classic pointer exercise with no overlap.

trees.notes: Builds on B08 recursion (multiple_recursive_calls, recursion_on_sequences) as B08's note asked. BST search carries pending concept:binary_search (B14) because it is the tree form of the same idea. Level-order traversal is graph_algorithms.breadth_first_search. Duplicate values in a BST go right and are not discussed further. general_trees uses isinstance as a copied line before B11/B12.

balanced_trees.notes: Red-black only (Boot.dev). Insert fix-up is traced, not implemented with parent pointers; rotations are written without parent pointers. Red-black deletion and AVL trees were left out.

tries.notes: Nested dicts with a '*' end marker, as in Boot.dev; plain functions instead of a Trie class, so no classes dependency.

graphs.notes: Graphs are dicts of sets/dicts and lists of lists, so no classes dependency. Examples iterate sorted(graph[v]) because set order of strings varies between runs.

graph_algorithms.notes: BFS/DFS/paths from Boot.dev; pagerank_iteration from py4e (introduced only). Weighted shortest paths (Dijkstra), topological sort and cycle detection in directed graphs are taught by none of the 8 courses and were left out. Uses `from collections import deque` (B07). Grid KPs build neighbour lists with plain loops.

hash_maps_internals.notes: Plain functions over a bucket list instead of Boot.dev's HashMap class, so no classes dependency. __hash__/__eq__ for user classes belongs to B11 dunder_methods. Average-case O(1) reasoning carries pending concept:complexity_big_o.

p_vs_np.notes: One topic: Boot.dev only, introduced. Exponential running time itself belongs to B14 complexity_big_o (pending).

topics.title: Nodes and links: walking a linked list
topics.summary: Link Node objects by their next attribute and walk the chain with a current pointer to print, count or search it, stopping at None.

knowledge_points.title: A node holds a value and a link to the next node
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.next = None

a = Node('a')
b = Node('b')
c = Node('c')
a.next = b
b.next = c
print(a.next.next.val)  # c
print(c.next)           # None
Each node stores its value and a reference to the next node; the last node's next is None.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what chains of .next and .val print for a hand-built list; draw the boxes-and-arrows picture for given code.

knowledge_points.title: Walk the list with a current pointer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
current = a
while current is not None:
    print(current.val)
    current = current.next
# a
# b
# c
Start at the head, use the node, then step to current.next; the loop ends when current becomes None. (Node and a, b, c as in KP1.)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed values for a traversal; reorder the lines of a traversal loop.

knowledge_points.title: Count and search while walking
knowledge_points.practice: Write sum_values(head) and index_of(head, target); predict results on an empty list (head is None).

knowledge_points.title: Traversal bugs: no step, lost head, missed last node
knowledge_points.worked_example:
current = a
while current.next is not None:
    print(current.val)
    current = current.next
# a
# b   <- c is never printed
Testing current.next stops one node early; forgetting current = current.next loops forever; moving the head variable itself loses the start of the list.
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the bug in three broken traversal loops; predict how many values each prints.

topics.title: Building a linked list: adding at the head and the tail
topics.summary: Grow a LinkedList by adding nodes at the head or the tail, keep a tail pointer, and handle the empty list.

knowledge_points.title: Add at the head: the new node points at the old head
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node class as defined earlier
head = None
for val in ['a', 'b', 'c']:
    node = Node(val)
    node.next = head
    head = node
print(head.val, head.next.val, head.next.next.val)  # c b a
Link the new node first, then move head to it; items added at the head come out in reverse order.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order after a series of head insertions; fix code that moves head before linking.

knowledge_points.title: Add at the tail by walking to the last node
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node class as defined earlier
def add_to_tail(head, val):
    node = Node(val)
    if head is None:
        return node
    current = head
    while current.next is not None:
        current = current.next
    current.next = node
    return head

head = None
for val in ['a', 'b', 'c']:
    head = add_to_tail(head, val)
print(head.val, head.next.next.val)  # a c
Here stopping at current.next is None is what we want: we need the last node, not None. An empty list needs its own case.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the loop condition that stops on the last node; predict results starting from an empty list.

knowledge_points.title: A LinkedList class that remembers its tail
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node as defined in nodes_and_traversal
class LinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None
        self.tail = None
    def add_to_tail(self, val):
        node = Node(val)
        if self.head is None:
            self.head = node
            self.tail = node
            return
        self.tail.next = node
        self.tail = node
    def to_list(self):
        out = []
        current = self.head
        while current is not None:
            out.append(current.val)
            current = current.next
        return out

items = LinkedList()
for val in ['a', 'b', 'c']:
    items.add_to_tail(val)
print(items.to_list(), items.tail.val)  # ['a', 'b', 'c'] c
Storing tail makes adding at the end one step instead of a walk; when the list is empty, head and tail both become the new node. to_list is the walk from nodes_and_traversal.
knowledge_points.practice: Write add_to_head(self, val) for the class, keeping tail correct when the list was empty; predict to_list() after mixed adds.

knowledge_points.title: Keeping head and tail in sync
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_to_tail(self, val):   # inside class LinkedList
        node = Node(val)
        if self.head is None:
            self.head = node
            return
        self.tail.next = node
        self.tail = node

items = LinkedList()
items.add_to_tail('a')
items.add_to_tail('b')  # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'next' ...
This add_to_tail forgot to set tail for the first node, so tail is still None on the second add. Every method must leave both head and tail correct.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot which method leaves head or tail wrong in buggy versions; trace head and tail through a sequence of adds.

topics.title: Removing nodes from a linked list
topics.summary: Remove the head node, remove the first node with a given value by relinking its neighbour, and keep head and tail right at the ends.

knowledge_points.title: Remove from the head
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node and LinkedList (with add_to_tail and to_list) as defined earlier
items = LinkedList()
for val in ['a', 'b', 'c']:
    items.add_to_tail(val)
old = items.head
items.head = old.next
print(old.val, items.to_list())  # a ['b', 'c']
Moving head one step forward drops the first node; save it first if you need its value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after removing from the head twice; write remove_from_head that returns the removed value.

knowledge_points.title: Remove from an empty or one-node list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# a new method inside class LinkedList:
    def remove_from_head(self):
        if self.head is None:
            return None
        old = self.head
        self.head = old.next
        if self.head is None:
            self.tail = None
        return old.val

items = LinkedList()
items.add_to_tail('a')
print(items.remove_from_head(), items.tail)  # a None
print(items.remove_from_head())             # None
Removing the only node must clear tail too; removing from an empty list returns None instead of crashing.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace head and tail through removals down to empty; fix a version that leaves tail pointing at a removed node.

knowledge_points.title: Remove a value from the middle: link around it
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the relinking line; predict the list after removing the first, middle and a missing value.

knowledge_points.title: Removing the last node must move tail
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(remove_value(items, 'c'), items.to_list(), items.tail.val)  # True ['a'] c
After removing 'c' the list is right but tail still points at the removed node, so the next add_to_tail would attach to it. Fix: if current is items.tail: items.tail = prev.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the bug that leaves tail stale; write the fixed remove_value and test it on all three positions.

topics.title: Reversing a linked list in place
topics.summary: Reverse a linked list by turning every next pointer around with prev, current and nxt pointers, tracing each step and avoiding losing the rest of the chain.

knowledge_points.title: Turn one arrow around without losing the rest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node class as defined earlier
a = Node('a')
b = Node('b')
a.next = b
nxt = a.next     # remember b first
a.next = None    # a now points backwards (to nothing)
b.next = a
print(b.val, b.next.val, a.next)  # b a None
Save the next node before overwriting next, or the rest of the list is unreachable.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the links after short pointer-assignment sequences; spot the line order that loses a node.

knowledge_points.title: The three-pointer loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node and LinkedList as defined earlier; items holds 1 -> 2 -> 3
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    current = head
    while current is not None:
        nxt = current.next
        current.next = prev
        prev = current
        current = nxt
    return prev

items.head = reverse(items.head)
print(items.to_list())  # [3, 2, 1]
Each pass flips one arrow and moves all three pointers one step; when current is None, prev is the new head.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table of prev, current and nxt for a 3-node list; reorder the four loop lines.

knowledge_points.title: Bugs: wrong order, forgotten new head
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# items holds 1 -> 2 -> 3 again; buggy version
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    current = head
    while current is not None:
        current.next = prev
        prev = current
        current = current.next
    return prev

items.head = reverse(items.head)
print(items.to_list())  # [1]
current.next was overwritten before it was saved, so the loop stops after one node. Also: the caller must store the returned head (and the old head becomes the tail).
knowledge_points.practice: Fix three broken reverse functions; predict what each buggy version leaves in the list.

topics.title: Linked lists vs Python lists: which operations are cheap
topics.summary: Count the steps each operation takes on a linked list and on a Python list, build a queue from a linked list with head and tail, and choose the right structure.

knowledge_points.title: Getting item i means walking i steps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Node and LinkedList (with add_to_tail and to_list) as defined earlier
def get(items, i):
    current = items.head
    for _ in range(i):
        current = current.next
    return current.val

items = LinkedList()
for val in 'abcde':
    items.add_to_tail(val)
print(get(items, 3))  # d, after 3 steps
A Python list jumps straight to index i; a linked list has no index, so reaching item i takes i steps.
knowledge_points.practice: Count the steps needed to reach given positions; choose which operations get slower as the list grows.

knowledge_points.title: Adding at the front: one step vs shifting everything
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [2, 3, 4]
nums.insert(0, 1)
print(nums)  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
insert(0, x) moves every existing item one place right (n moves); a linked list's add_to_head relinks one node no matter how long the list is.
knowledge_points.practice: Count moves for insert(0, x) on lists of given lengths versus the linked-list version; multiple choice on which is cheaper for given operations.

knowledge_points.title: A queue built from a linked list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# LinkedList with add_to_tail and remove_from_head from the previous topics
q = LinkedList()
for name in ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']:
    q.add_to_tail(name)
print(q.remove_from_head(), q.to_list())  # ana ['bo', 'cy']
Join at the tail, leave from the head: both are one step, which is how deque stays fast at both ends.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a linked-list queue through joins and serves; write a stack using add_to_head and remove_from_head.

knowledge_points.title: Choose the structure for the job
knowledge_points.worked_example: Many reads by position: Python list. Many adds/removes at the front: deque (or a linked list). Many adds/removes at both ends plus occasional scans: deque. In everyday Python you use list and deque; you write a linked list to understand them.
knowledge_points.practice: For each described workload, choose list, deque or a hand-written linked list and justify with the step counts.

topics.title: Binary trees: nodes, children and tree words
topics.summary: Build a binary tree from TreeNode objects with left and right children, name its parts (root, leaf, parent, subtree, depth) and follow paths to a node.

knowledge_points.title: A node with a left and a right child
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

root = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(3), TreeNode(8, None, TreeNode(9)))
print(root.left.val, root.right.right.val)  # 3 9
print(root.left.left)                      # None
Like a linked-list node, but with two links; a missing child is None.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values reached by chains of .left/.right; write the constructor call for a drawn tree.

knowledge_points.title: Tree words: root, parent, child, leaf, subtree, depth
knowledge_points.worked_example:
root = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(4)), TreeNode(8, None, TreeNode(9)))

node = root.left
print(node.left is None and node.right is None)  # False: 3 has children 1 and 4
leaf = root.left.right
print(leaf.left is None and leaf.right is None)  # True: 4 is a leaf
Root 5 has depth 0; 3 and 8 are its children (depth 1); 1, 4 and 9 are leaves. Each child is the root of its own subtree.
knowledge_points.practice: Name the root, leaves and parents in drawn trees; give the depth of named nodes; test whether a node is a leaf.

knowledge_points.title: Following a path, and falling off the tree
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where a path of L/R steps ends or whether it crashes; fix a path-follower that does not check for None.

topics.title: Recursive functions on trees: count, sum, max and height
topics.summary: Write tree functions with an empty-tree base case and two recursive calls: count nodes, add values, find the greatest value, count leaves and measure height.

knowledge_points.title: Count nodes: empty tree is the base case
knowledge_points.practice: Write total(node) summing all values; predict count() on small drawn trees.

knowledge_points.title: Greatest value: combine results with max
knowledge_points.practice: Write smallest(node); fix a greatest() that returns 0 for an empty tree and test it on negative values.

knowledge_points.title: Height: the longest path down
knowledge_points.practice: Predict heights of drawn trees, including a one-sided chain; trace the calls for a 3-node tree.

knowledge_points.title: Two base cases: counting leaves
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function counting nodes with exactly one child; fix a leaves() whose missing None check crashes.

topics.title: Visiting every node: preorder, inorder and postorder
topics.summary: List a tree's values in preorder, inorder and postorder by placing the node before, between or after its subtrees, and pick the order a task needs.

knowledge_points.title: Preorder: the node first
knowledge_points.practice: Write the preorder list for drawn trees; predict the output of preorder().

knowledge_points.title: Inorder and postorder: move the node
knowledge_points.practice: Give all three orders for drawn trees; fill in the return line for a named order.

knowledge_points.title: Reconstruct facts from an order
knowledge_points.worked_example: In preorder the first value is always the root; in postorder the last value is. Given preorder [7, 2, 9] of a 3-node tree, 7 is the root.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify the root and leaves from given traversal lists; decide which order produced a given list.

knowledge_points.title: Choosing the order for a job
knowledge_points.worked_example:
root = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(4)), TreeNode(8, None, TreeNode(9)))

def print_outline(node, depth=0):
    if node is None:
        return
    print('  ' * depth + str(node.val))
    print_outline(node.left, depth + 1)
    print_outline(node.right, depth + 1)

print_outline(root)
# 5
#   3
#     1
#     4
#   8
#     9
Printing an outline or copying a tree needs parents first (preorder); freeing or totalling folder sizes needs children first (postorder).
knowledge_points.practice: Match tasks to traversal orders; write an outline printer that also shows depth numbers.

topics.title: Trees with any number of children: org charts and folders
topics.summary: Represent a tree whose nodes hold a list of children (an org chart, a folder tree) and write recursive functions that loop over the children.

knowledge_points.title: A node with a list of children
knowledge_points.worked_example:
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, reports):
        self.name = name
        self.reports = reports

boss = Employee('Ada', [Employee('Bo', [Employee('Cy', [])]), Employee('Di', [])])
print(boss.reports[0].name, boss.reports[1].name)  # Bo Di
Instead of left and right, each node keeps a list; a leaf has an empty list.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict names reached through .reports indexes; build a small org chart from a description.

knowledge_points.title: Recursion with a loop over children
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def count_staff(e):
    total = 1
    for r in e.reports:
        total += count_staff(r)
    return total

print(count_staff(boss))  # 4
No explicit None check is needed: a leaf's empty list means the loop does nothing and the function returns 1.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function returning everyone under a manager (Helsinki's 'bosses and subordinates'); predict counts for subtrees.

knowledge_points.title: A tree made of nested dicts
knowledge_points.practice: Write a function counting files in a nested-dict folder tree; trace total_size on a 2-level example.

topics.title: Binary search trees: searching and inserting
topics.summary: Use the BST ordering rule to recognise valid search trees, find a value by going left or right, insert new values recursively, and find the minimum and maximum.

knowledge_points.title: The BST rule: smaller left, larger right
knowledge_points.worked_example: In a binary search tree every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in its right subtree is larger. 5 with left child 3 and right child 8 is valid; 5 with a 6 anywhere under its left child is not.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether drawn trees are valid BSTs, including the trap where a grandchild breaks the rule; place a value in the right spot.

knowledge_points.title: Search: one comparison per level
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the nodes visited when searching for given values; write a recursive version of exists().

knowledge_points.title: Insert: walk down and attach a new leaf
knowledge_points.practice: Draw the tree built by inserting a sequence; fix an insert that forgets return node.

knowledge_points.title: Minimum and maximum: keep going left or right
knowledge_points.practice: Write get_max; predict min and max for trees built from given sequences.

topics.title: Binary search trees: sorted order and deleting
topics.summary: Get a BST's values in sorted order with inorder traversal, and delete a value in each of the three cases: a leaf, one child, two children.

knowledge_points.title: Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted
knowledge_points.worked_example:
root = None
for v in [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 9]:
    root = insert(root, v)
print(inorder(root))  # [1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9]
Left subtree (smaller) first, then the node, then the right subtree (larger): sorted order falls out of the rule.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict inorder output for trees built from sequences; use it to check whether a tree is a valid BST.

knowledge_points.title: Delete a leaf or a node with one child
knowledge_points.practice: Draw the tree after deleting given leaves and one-child nodes; fill in the two replacement lines.

knowledge_points.title: Delete a node with two children: borrow the successor
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# delete() as in KP2, with these lines added after the one-child cases:
        succ = node.right
        while succ.left is not None:
            succ = succ.left
        node.val = succ.val
        node.right = delete(node.right, succ.val)

# tree built from 5, 3, 8, 7, 9
root = delete(root, 5)
print(root.val, inorder(root))  # 7 [3, 7, 8, 9]
Copy in the smallest value of the right subtree (the next value in sorted order), then delete that value from the right subtree, which is an easy case.
knowledge_points.practice: Name the successor of given nodes; draw the tree after deleting a two-child node; check the result with inorder.

topics.title: Why trees need balancing
topics.summary: See that inserting sorted data turns a BST into a chain, compare the height of balanced and unbalanced trees, and check whether a tree is height-balanced.

knowledge_points.title: Sorted input builds a chain
knowledge_points.worked_example:
root = None
for v in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    root = insert(root, v)
print(height(root))  # 4

root = None
for v in [3, 1, 4, 2, 5]:
    root = insert(root, v)
print(height(root))  # 2
Same five values, different insert order: in sorted order every node goes right, so the tree is just a linked list.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the height after inserting given sequences; choose which insert order gives the tallest tree.

knowledge_points.title: Height decides the search cost
knowledge_points.worked_example:
levels = 0
nodes = 1
while nodes < 1_000_000:
    levels += 1
    nodes = 2 ** (levels + 1) - 1
print(levels)  # 19
A full tree of height h holds 2**(h+1) - 1 nodes, so a million values fit in height 19: about 20 comparisons per search, versus up to a million in a chain.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute the most comparisons a search needs in balanced and chain-shaped trees of given sizes.

knowledge_points.title: Checking balance at every node
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which drawn trees are balanced; fix an is_balanced that only checks the root.

topics.title: Red-black trees: the colouring rules
topics.summary: State and check the red-black rules (black root, no red node with a red child, the same number of black nodes on every path down) and explain why they keep the tree short.

knowledge_points.title: Every node is red or black
knowledge_points.worked_example:
RED, BLACK = 'red', 'black'

class RBNode:
    def __init__(self, val, color, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.color = color
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

root = RBNode(5, BLACK, RBNode(3, RED), RBNode(8, RED))
print(root.color, root.left.color)  # black red
A red-black tree is a BST whose nodes carry a colour; the colours are only bookkeeping that limits how lopsided the tree may get.
knowledge_points.practice: Read colours off code-built trees; mark which drawn trees are valid BSTs before looking at colours.

knowledge_points.title: Rule check: black root and no red-red
knowledge_points.practice: Find the rule each drawn tree breaks; fill in the condition in red_red().

knowledge_points.title: Equal black height on every path
knowledge_points.practice: Count black nodes on each path of drawn trees; decide whether a tree passes the rule.

knowledge_points.title: Why the rules keep the tree short
knowledge_points.worked_example: With no two reds in a row and equal blacks on every path, the longest path (alternating black and red) is at most twice the shortest (all black). So height stays about 2 * log2(n): roughly 40 levels for a million values instead of a million.
knowledge_points.practice: Give the longest possible path for a given black height; compare worst-case heights of a plain BST and a red-black tree.

topics.title: Rotations and fixing a red-black tree after insert
topics.summary: Rotate a subtree left or right while keeping BST order, and trace how a red-black insert recolours or rotates to restore the rules.

knowledge_points.title: Rotate left: the right child moves up
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# TreeNode, insert, inorder and height as defined earlier
def rotate_left(x):
    y = x.right
    x.right = y.left
    y.left = x
    return y

root = None
for v in [1, 2, 3]:
    root = insert(root, v)
root = rotate_left(root)
print(root.val, root.left.val, root.right.val)  # 2 1 3
y's old left subtree moves across to become x's right subtree; the parent must store the returned new root.
knowledge_points.practice: Draw the tree after a left rotation at a named node; reorder the three relinking lines.

knowledge_points.title: Rotate right is the mirror image
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# TreeNode, insert, inorder and height as defined earlier
def rotate_right(y):
    x = y.left
    y.left = x.right
    x.right = y
    return x

root = None
for v in [3, 2, 1]:
    root = insert(root, v)
root = rotate_right(root)
print(inorder(root), height(root))  # [1, 2, 3] 1
A rotation changes the shape and height but never the inorder (sorted) order.
knowledge_points.practice: Write rotate_right from rotate_left; check with inorder that a rotation kept BST order.

knowledge_points.title: Insert red, then fix: recolour when the uncle is red
knowledge_points.worked_example: New nodes are inserted red (keeps black heights equal). If the parent is also red and the uncle (parent's sibling) is red: make parent and uncle black, grandparent red, and repeat the check from the grandparent. Finally colour the root black.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace colours after inserts that trigger recolouring; say which rule was broken before each fix.

knowledge_points.title: Rotate when the uncle is black
knowledge_points.worked_example: Insert 1, 2, 3 into an empty red-black tree: 3's parent 2 is red and its uncle is empty (black), so rotate left at 1 and swap colours: 2 becomes the black root with red children 1 and 3. A zig-zag case needs two rotations.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace inserting short sequences, naming each fix (recolour, single rotation, double rotation) and the resulting tree.

topics.title: Tries: storing words letter by letter
topics.summary: Store words in a trie made of nested dicts with an end-of-word marker, and check whether a word or a prefix is present.

knowledge_points.title: Insert one word as a path of nested dicts
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the nested dict after inserting a word; fill in the line that steps one level down.

knowledge_points.title: Words share their prefixes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# insert(trie, word) as defined earlier
trie = {}
for w in ['cat', 'car', 'cow']:
    insert(trie, w)
print(list(trie['c'].keys()))       # ['a', 'o']
print(list(trie['c']['a'].keys()))  # ['t', 'r']

knowledge_points.title: Longest common prefix
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# insert(trie, word) as defined earlier
def common_prefix(trie):
    node = trie
    prefix = ''
    while len(node) == 1 and '*' not in node:
        ch = list(node.keys())[0]
        prefix += ch
        node = node[ch]
    return prefix

trie = {}

topics.title: How a dict finds a key: hashing to an index
topics.summary: Explain why a list index is instant but searching is not, turn a key into a list index with a hash function and %, store and fetch pairs in a bucket list, and predict how Python's hash() treats keys.

knowledge_points.title: Index access is one step; searching is many
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pairs = [('ana', 31), ('bo', 27), ('cy', 40)]
for name, age in pairs:
    if name == 'cy':
        print(age)  # 40, after checking 3 pairs
ages = [31, 27, 40]
print(ages[2])  # 40, in one step
A list stores items side by side, so position i is found by arithmetic. Finding a key means checking items one by one, unless the key can be turned into a position.
knowledge_points.practice: Count how many comparisons a search makes in lists of given sizes; choose which lookups take the same time for any size.

knowledge_points.title: A hash function turns a key into an index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def key_to_index(key, size):
    total = 0
    for ch in key:
        total += ord(ch)
    return total % size

print(key_to_index('abc', 8))  # 6
print(key_to_index('bo', 8))   # 1
Add up the character codes (97 + 98 + 99 = 294), then % size keeps the result between 0 and size - 1. The same key always gives the same index.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute indexes for short keys and table sizes; fill in the line that keeps the index in range.

knowledge_points.title: Store and fetch in a bucket list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# key_to_index(key, size) as defined earlier
buckets = [None] * 8

def put(key, value):
    buckets[key_to_index(key, len(buckets))] = (key, value)

def get(key):
    item = buckets[key_to_index(key, len(buckets))]
    if item is None or item[0] != key:
        return None
    return item[1]

put('bo', 27)
print(get('bo'), buckets[1], get('cy'))  # 27 ('bo', 27) None
Store the key with the value, so get can check it found the right key; a real dict raises KeyError where this returns None.

topics.title: Collisions: when two keys want the same slot
topics.summary: Recognise collisions, see how naive storing overwrites data, and handle them with chaining (a list per bucket) and with linear probing.

knowledge_points.title: Two keys, one index
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# key_to_index(key, size) as defined earlier
print(key_to_index('abc', 8), key_to_index('cab', 8))  # 6 6
Different keys can produce the same index (here, the same letters). With more keys than slots, a collision is guaranteed.
knowledge_points.practice: Find colliding pairs among given keys; predict what a one-item-per-slot table holds after colliding puts.

knowledge_points.title: Chaining: each bucket holds a list of pairs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# key_to_index(key, size) as defined earlier
buckets = [[] for _ in range(8)]

def put(key, value):
    bucket = buckets[key_to_index(key, len(buckets))]
    for i in range(len(bucket)):
        if bucket[i][0] == key:
            bucket[i] = (key, value)
            return
    bucket.append((key, value))

put('abc', 1)
put('cab', 2)
put('abc', 3)
print(buckets[6])  # [('abc', 3), ('cab', 2)]
Search the bucket for the key: replace it if present (keys stay unique), otherwise append. Use [[] for _ in range(8)], not [[]] * 8, which shares one list.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace buckets through puts with collisions and updates; write get() for the chained table.

knowledge_points.title: Linear probing: try the next slot
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# key_to_index(key, size) as defined earlier
slots = [None] * 8

def put(key, value):
    i = key_to_index(key, len(slots))
    while slots[i] is not None and slots[i][0] != key:
        i = (i + 1) % len(slots)
    slots[i] = (key, value)

put('abc', 1)
put('cab', 2)
print(slots[6], slots[7])  # ('abc', 1) ('cab', 2)
If the slot is taken by another key, step to the next one, wrapping around with %. get() must follow the same steps until it finds the key or an empty slot.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace slot indexes for colliding puts including wrap-around; write the matching get().

knowledge_points.title: Bad hash functions cause many collisions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def bad_index(key, size):
    return len(key) % size

for k in ['ana', 'bob', 'cyd']:
    print(k, bad_index(k, 8))
# ana 3
# bob 3
# cyd 3
If many keys land in one bucket, every lookup searches a long list and the table is no faster than a list of pairs. Good hashes spread keys evenly.
knowledge_points.practice: Compare collision counts of two hash functions on a key list; choose which hash function is better for given data.

knowledge_points.title: Load factor: how full is the table?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
count = 6
size = 8
print(count / size)  # 0.75
Load factor = stored keys / slots. As it rises, collisions and probe chains grow; probing tables are full at 1.0.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute load factors; decide when a table with a 0.7 limit must grow.

knowledge_points.title: Resize: a bigger table and re-insert everything
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# key_to_index(key, size) as defined earlier
old = [[('abc', 1), ('cab', 2)], [('b', 5)]]
new = [[] for _ in range(8)]
for bucket in old:
    for key, value in bucket:
        new[key_to_index(key, len(new))].append((key, value))
print(new[6], new[2])  # [('abc', 1), ('cab', 2)] [('b', 5)]
Every key's index depends on the table size, so each pair must be hashed again into the new table.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace where keys land after resizing from 4 to 8 slots; write resize() for a chained table.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: copying buckets to the same positions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# key_to_index(key, size) as defined earlier
new = [[] for _ in range(8)]
new[0] = [('b', 5)]  # copied from old slot 0 of a size-2 table
print(key_to_index('b', 8))  # 2: get('b') looks in slot 2 and finds nothing
Copying without rehashing leaves keys where lookups no longer look, so they appear to vanish.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the bug in a broken resize; predict which keys a lookup can still find afterwards.

knowledge_points.title: Why lookups stay fast on average
knowledge_points.worked_example:
size, moves = 1, 0
for n in range(1, 1025):
    if n > size:
        moves += size
        size *= 2
print(size, moves)  # 1024 1023
Doubling when full means 1024 inserts cause only 1023 extra moves in total, about one per insert. With a low load factor most buckets hold 0 or 1 keys, so lookups take a few steps however big the dict is.
